Chitral town and Booni (the Upper Chitral hub) are the reliable fuel points on this corridor. Mastuj, Sor Laspur, and the Shandur Pass area itself are small settlements with thin infrastructure — fill up fully at Booni before continuing toward Shandur or into the Yarkhun/Broghil direction.

Neelum Valley:

Muzaffarabad is the main hub. Athmuqam and Kel have basic bazaars and likely fuel, but Taobat (the last village in the valley) and the jeep tracks off the main road (toward Ratti Gali, Arang Kel, Chitta Katta) don't — fill up in Athmuqam or Kel before pushing further up-valley.

The general pattern across every remote jeep-track valley on this list (Chapursan, Shimshal, Naltar, Bilamik/Thorsay, Madaglasht, Hushe): fuel exists in the last KKH/main-road town before the turnoff (Sost for Chapursan, Karimabad/Shishkat area for Shimshal, Nomal for Naltar, the Skardu-road towns for Bilamik, Chitral town for Madaglasht, Khaplu for Hushe) and nowhere beyond it. Treat every side-valley turnoff in this entire document as "last fuel here" unless a specific entry says otherwise.

Connectivity, cash, and seasonal road closures

SIM/network: SCOM is Gilgit-Baltistan's own network and generally has the best coverage in- region — already noted for Neelum specifically but worth knowing as a general rule across GB, not just AJK. Major national networks (Jazz, Zong, Telenor, Ufone) have patchy coverage once you're off the KKH/main roads, and several specific spots in this document (Chapursan, Hushe past Saicho, most

multi-day treks) have no signal at all — that's noted at point of use throughout.

Cash: ATMs exist in Gilgit, Skardu, Hunza (Karimabad/Aliabad), Chitral town, and Mingora — not much beyond that. Carry enough cash for each region's leg before heading into the valleys; jeep hire, guesthouses, and local guides are almost entirely cash transactions.

Seasonal closures, consolidated: Babusar Pass (Kaghan-to-Gilgit link) closes with first winter snow, reopens ~May; Shandur Pass (Chitral-to-Gilgit link) is summer-only; Deosai's road closes to vehicles roughly November-May; Lowari is now tunneled year-round so less of a concern than it used to be, though the old pass itself is still summer-only for those specifically chasing that route. Most individual trek season windows (May/June- September) are already noted per entry — this is just the connecting-road picture.

Fuel guide — where to refuel, and the long gaps

between pumps

The single biggest practical gap in this whole document until now. On a 125cc bike especially, running out mid-gap isn't a minor inconvenience — some of these stretches have no settlements at all, so plan every fill-up around these gaps rather than assuming "there'll be something eventually."

KKH corridor (Islamabad → Hunza → Khunjerab):

Mansehra has a service station; the next one is at Thakot, about 70km further — fill up in Mansehra even if you're not empty.

Besham (290km from Islamabad) is the last major petrol stop before the mountain gorges begin — top off here regardless of your gauge; the ~210km

stretch to Chilas is remote and slow-going, not a place to be searching for fuel.

Chilas (500km) has a named pump — Gunar Farm Chilas — with the next one at Jaglot.

Gilgit (610km) and Karimabad/Hunza (700km) are both reliable fuel hubs with multiple pumps.

Passu (770km) has limited options — fill up in Karimabad/Aliabad before heading further up- valley if you're continuing toward Sost/Khunjerab.

Sost (810km) is the last Pakistani town before the Khunjerab border and has reliable fuel — this is your last chance before the pass.

Sost → Khunjerab Pass (~75-90km one-way) has no fuel whatsoever — this is a there-and-back stretch from Sost for most riders (day trip up to the pass and back), so fill up completely in Sost before making the run.

Kaghan Valley → Babusar → Chilas:

Fill your tank in Naran — there is no petrol pump after Batakundi (12km past Naran), all the way over Babusar Top and down to Chilas — that's roughly 90-100km with nothing.

This is one of the least forgiving gaps on your whole list precisely because it's also a high pass (4,173m) — don't attempt it on a low tank even if you think you can coast down the Chilas side.

Astore / Deosai / Skardu:

Astore valley entrance has a fuel stop — fill up completely here.

There is no fuel option from Chillam through Deosai all the way to Skardu city — this is a genuinely long, high-altitude gap (100km+) with zero settlements offering fuel. Confirmed by an actual motorbike trip report (Suzuki GS-150), not just a general guide — take it seriously.

Between Skardu and Khaplu, there's only one fuel station, at Ghawari — relevant if you're doing the Khaplu/Hushe leg of Region 2.

Swat/Kalam → Kumrat:

Kalam is the last town with reliable fuel infrastructure. Utror and Thal (the gateway to Kumrat/Jahaz Banda) are both described as small villages with only basic amenities — don't count on fuel past Kalam. Fill up there before heading to Utror, Gabral, Mahodand, or over Badgoi Pass toward Kumrat.

Chitral → Shandur/Booni/Mastuj:

Snow Lake & Hispar La Trek

What it is: A 16km-wide glacial basin at 4,800m where the Biafo and Hispar glaciers meet, connecting Hunza (west) to Baltistan (east) via the Hispar La pass — this is genuinely a cross-region expedition, not a Hunza-only trek.

Two directions: Most groups start from Askole (Skardu side) and finish in Hispar village (Hunza/Nagar side), or occasionally the reverse.

Distance/duration: About 190 km total, 12 days classic itinerary, though full trips including travel run around 3 weeks door to door, with 12 days of high-altitude trekking.

Elevation: Hispar Pass tops out at 5,150m. Difficulty: Strenuous, remote, requires a certified guide and full camping/porter support — no shortcuts here, and no bike or bus gets anywhere near it.

Season: June–September only.

Note for later: we'll cover the Skardu-side approach (Askole, Baltoro) properly when we get to Region 2.

Chapursan Valley & Baldiyat Meadows

Route: KKH to Sost (last town before Khunjerab) → turn off onto the Chapursan valley road → Zood Khun (last village).

Distance/time: About a 4-hour jeep ride from Sost to Zood Khun; roughly 6 hours total from Karimabad, 8 from Gilgit. The Sost–Chapursan road is narrow and rough — not one to underestimate on a loaded bike; go slow and consider it jeep territory past the first villages.

Local transport: One public jeep a day runs the valley, leaving Zood Khun around 5:30–6am — good to know if you're not self-driving.

What's there: Baba Ghundi Shrine (2 hrs beyond Zood Khun), Yishkok Meadow (base for treks toward Yashkuk Yaz Glacier and Sakar Sar base camp, the valley's highest peak at 6,272m), and several scattered Wakhi villages.

Accommodation: Guesthouses and homestays in Zood Khun and nearby villages — basic but authentic Wakhi hospitality.

Best time: June–August, when meadows are in bloom and trails are most accessible. Expect no reliable signal or WiFi once you're past Sost — worth knowing if you're planning to vlog live.

Culture note: If your timing lines up (June– September), Kyrgyz traders sometimes cross from Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor via the Irshad Pass to trade at Chapursan — and there's an annual two-

day Baba Ghundi Festival with traditional games like buzkashi.

Hushe Valley — the other big trekking hub

(K6/K7, Laila Peak, Masherbrum/K1)

Hushe is to Baltistan's technical trekking what Minapin is to Hunza's — one road-end village feeding several serious objectives. Route in: Skardu → jeep via Khaplu, Machulo, Kanday, Khaney → Hushe (the highest permanent village in the area, ~3,050m). All multi-day treks above the village require a CKNP trekking permit, issued at the Skardu CKNP office; porters are hired directly from Hushe through the village porters' association. Homestays and one or two basic guesthouses exist in the village itself; everything above it is tent camping. Mobile signal is patchy in Hushe and nonexistent past Saicho junction — same vlogging- connectivity note as Chapursan in Region 1.

K6/K7 Base Camp Trek (Charakusa Valley) — this covers "Charkusa Valley Husha" from your original list too: Hushe → Saicho (4-5 hrs) → across the Charakusa Glacier → K6/K7 Base Camp at 4,550- 4,600m. 8-10 days total, no technical climbing needed for the base camp itself — genuinely one of the more accessible "serious" treks in this whole region, similar difficulty tier to Patundas in Hunza. K6 stands 7,282m, K7 stands 6,934m, and you'll

also see Laila Peak and Link Sar from the same basin.

Laila Peak Base Camp Trek: Same Saicho/Charakusa approach as above, branching toward the Gondogoro drainage. Laila Peak (6,237m/6,400m depending on source) is widely considered the single most photogenic peak in the Karakoram — a near-perfect pyramid. Masherbrum Base Camp Trek (K1): Hushe → Barbisan (3-4 hrs) → Brumbrama/Parbisan (3-4 hrs) → Masherbrum Base Camp at 4,200-4,350m (3-4 hrs). About 2 nights out from the village, moderate difficulty, no technical skills required for the base camp — Masherbrum itself (7,821m) is a genuine 4,000m granite wall and one of the most demanding technical peaks in Pakistan to actually summit, but the base camp trek is very achievable.

Season: June-September for all three, same as everywhere else in Baltistan.

Gilgit city

Mostly a waypoint and transport hub rather than a destination in itself — this is where the Hunza road, Skardu road, Naltar turnoff, and Astore turnoff all converge. Gilgit sits about 60km from Astore and roughly 2 hours from Naltar. You've effectively already covered getting here in Region 1's Hunza route section, since Gilgit sits on the same KKH corridor just before the Hunza turnoff. Food-wise, same note as Astore — this is the same broader GB food culture covered in Regions 1 and 2, not a distinct cuisine of its own.

Naltar Valley (fuller treatment — you've already

seen Sheesha Lake here)

Route: Gilgit → Nomal village (turn off the KKH) → Naltar Bala (Upper Naltar), about 34-40km, 1.5-2 hours. The road to Naltar Bala itself is manageable; the lakes beyond require a separate 4x4 jeep leg — old Willys jeeps with reinforced suspension are the standard local vehicle for this stretch, and taking your own vehicle (bike included) isn't advisable for the final rocky, boulder-strewn section.

The lakes: Collectively called the Naltar Lakes or Bashkiri Lakes — Satrangi Lake (Bashkiri I, the famous "seven-colored" one, named for the mix of hues from moss and underwater vegetation), Blue Lake (Bashkiri II, 1km from Satrangi), and Feroza Lake (Bashkiri III), roughly 12-17km from Naltar Bala depending on source.

Jeep costs: Round-trip jeep hire to the lakes runs roughly PKR 15,000-16,000 from Nomal, or about PKR 20,000 one-way if starting the whole trip from Gilgit.

Ski resort: Naltar has Pakistan's oldest ski resort (the other being Malam Jabba in Swat), run largely by the Pakistan Air Force, which introduced skiing here — worth knowing if you're ever up this way in winter instead of summer, since most of this whole document assumes a summer trekking season.

Turgil Meadows recap: as covered back in Region 1 — about a 2-hour trek from upper Naltar, views of Rakaposhi and Diran.

Season: May-October for the lakes/valley in general; winter for skiing.

Buskochi (Baskochi) Top

Start point: Shishkat village (near Attabad Lake) — bike-accessible.

Route: A 3–4 hour round trip through light forest and traditional Gojal farmland, up to panoramic views of Attabad Lake and the surrounding villages. Difficulty: Easy — a "hidden gem for those who love nature without the burn," good for a late start, sunset trek, or mellow day with local guides.

Good fit for: a half-day add-on if you're already based near Attabad/Hunza and want a viewpoint hike without committing to a full trek day.

Turgil Meadows (Naltar)

What it is: A meadow high in upper Naltar with views of Rakaposhi and Diran in the distance, about a 2-hour trek from upper Naltar.

Geography note: Naltar Valley is technically reached via Nomal (off the KKH before Hunza proper) and administratively sits closer to Gilgit district than Hunza — I'm covering it here since you already know Naltar from your Sheesha Lake visit, but I'll give it fuller treatment (Naltar Lakes/Bashkiri/Satrangi, the ski resort, Naltar- Pakora trek) alongside Kohistan/Gilgit-corridor spots in a later region.

Kho Nagar Valley (Miacher Kho Meadows) —

added after correcting an earlier misplacement

What it is: "Kho Nagar Valley" from your original list is Miacher Kho Meadows (also just called Kho Meadows), a meadow above Miacher village in Nagar Valley — genuinely in Region 1's territory, not Kohistan as I'd first guessed while researching Region 4. Route: Gilgit → Nagar → Minapin → Miacher village → Kho Meadows, about 3-4 hours total from Gilgit City. A short ~30 minute walk from the parking area up to the meadow itself.

Bike note: Explicitly bike-friendly — the source guide's only caution is to tie down luggage tightly given the road condition, unlike most of the harder- to-reach spots in this region. Good road from the KKH turnoff.

What's there: Views toward Diran Peak, Rakaposhi, Hunza's Duikar viewpoint, Hapakun Meadows, and Rakaposhi Base Camp — essentially a lower-effort viewpoint over the same peaks Rakaposhi Base Camp trekkers work much harder to see. Good fit for: an easy day trip if you're already in Minapin for Rakaposhi Base Camp and want a lighter add-on, or a standalone half-day out of Gilgit/Nagar.

REGION 1: Hunza–Nagar–Gojal

Corridor

Getting there from Islamabad/Rawalpindi

By bike: ~600–650 km on the Karakoram Highway (N- 35). Two options:

Year-round route: Islamabad → Hazara Motorway → Mansehra → Besham → Dasu (Kohistan) → Chilas → Gilgit → Hunza. This is the only option outside summer.

Naran–Babusar route (May–Oct only): Islamabad → Mansehra → Balakot → Naran → Babusar Top (4,173m) → Chilas → Gilgit → Hunza. Shorter and far more scenic, but Babusar closes with the first snow, and it's a serious high-altitude pass on a 125cc — go in daylight, watch fuel.

Realistic riding time: 14–20 hours of actual road time. Nobody sane does this in one day on a bike — plan 2 days with an overnight in Besham/Chilas/Naran, or 3 if you want to actually enjoy it.

Fuel stops: Mansehra, Besham, Chilas, Gilgit all have pumps; nothing reliable in between on the KKH stretch, so fill up at every town.

The KKH has been largely improved under CPEC, but sections after Chilas can still be narrow and winding.

By local bus: NATCO (government-run, Northern Areas Transport Corporation) is the main operator, with Faisal Movers and Silk Route also running the route now.

Islamabad/Rawalpindi → Gilgit: PKR 3,760; Islamabad/Rawalpindi → Hunza: PKR 5,040. Fares have crept up through 2026 — some listings now show PKR 5,500+ on the AC Yutong buses.

Travel time is around 13–14 hours on the newer express services, though 16–20 hours is more typical with rest stops.

Faisal Movers specifically (you asked about this one): runs Islamabad → Hunza directly, PKR 4,500–5,000 depending on class. Departure from Pirwadhai Crystal Lines Terminal in Islamabad/Rawalpindi (or the "26-number" terminal) — book ahead in peak season, seats sell out. Their Gilgit-end terminal is on Shahr-e-Quaid-e- Azam, near the NATCO terminal, opposite Skyways — contact 0311-1224488 for booking/timing queries. Return departures from Gilgit run between 12:00pm and 8:00pm.

From Gilgit onward to Karimabad: frequent shared vans/Hiace/Suzuki wagons, roughly 2 hours, cheap (a few hundred PKR).

If you ever need a second/backup bike here: rental shops cluster around Jutial in Gilgit and Aliabad in Hunza — see the Practical Reference Guide at the top of this document for named operators (Pakistan Bikers, AMT Expeditions) and rates.

Two corrections found while researching this region

Musa ka Musalla — actually in Mansehra District (Siran Valley/Kaghan junction), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — nowhere near Astore or Gilgit-

Baltistan at all. It's a 4,080m peak reached via Shinkiari → Manda Gucha, a separate 3-4 day trek in its own right. Will cover properly in the Kaghan- Naran-Kashmir region.

Sheitan Gawt Lake — actually in Bahrain Valley, Swat (near Kedam village), not Astore. Will cover in the Swat-Kalam-Kumrat region.

Region 3 is now fully covered.

REGION 4: Gilgit–Naltar–Kohistan

Corridor

Getting there

This is the corridor you already pass through on the way to every other region — Kohistan sits between Besham and Chilas on the KKH, and Gilgit sits right where the Hunza road, Skardu road, Naltar turnoff, and Astore turnoff all meet. If you've already done Region 1's Hunza trip, you've driven through most of this corridor already; this section fills in the side-trips you'd have passed without stopping.

Kohistan — Palas Valley (Morro Meadows & Takhto Lake)

Route: Islamabad → Besham (4-5 hours) → Dobair Bazaar (~15km further) → Pattan (~25km further,

on the KKH) → cross the Indus bridge at Pattan → jeep track into Palas Valley. Kolai-Palas is its own district now, split from the rest of Kohistan, divided into accessible Lower Palas and the harder-to- reach Upper Palas.

Morro (Morro/Morroo) Meadows: From Pattan, a jeep track leads to the village of Khalyar/Shiryal/Mudu (sources vary on the exact village name and route details — this is a genuinely under-documented area), then a trek of roughly 7- 8km with about 1,900m of cumulative elevation gain, taking 3-7 hours depending on the exact route and source. Locals are described as helpful with guiding and porters, though this is not a formal tourism setup — expect to arrange things informally on arrival rather than booking anything in advance.

Takhto Lake (also called Takhto Sar Lake): Also in the Palas Valley cluster, described as one of the least-explored alpine lakes in Pakistan — visited by at least one Pakistani motorbike tour operator specifically as an exploratory trip, which tells you how off the beaten path this still is. I couldn't find hard distance/elevation figures for this one specifically; treat it as bundled with the Morro Meadows trip into the same general Palas Valley area, and expect to figure out final logistics locally.

Bike note: the jeep track from Pattan into Palas Valley is exactly that — a jeep track. Kohistan's

back valleys are some of the least developed for tourism in this entire list, so don't expect the infrastructure (or road quality) you'd find in Hunza or even Kaghan.

Gear rental & general mechanics

Gear rental in Islamabad: Ascender Outdoors — trekking gear sales and rental (tents, sleeping bags, stoves, crampons, ice axes), F-11/1, Ali Market, Islamabad, +92 333 9980903, info@ascender.pk. Worth stocking up here before heading north rather than counting on finding gear in-valley.

Gear rental in-trek: several specific treks in this document already note local rental (e.g. camping gear at Rakaposhi Base Camp for ~PKR 3,000/night) — those are noted at point of use rather than repeated here.

Mechanics/fuel beyond bike rental shops: every KKH town (Mansehra, Besham, Chilas, Gilgit, Karimabad) and every Swat/Kaghan hub (Mingora, Balakot, Naran, Kalam) has basic mechanics and fuel — mechanics are available in main towns only, so carry basic tools and a spare tube past those points. Past the last town before a jeep track, you're relying on the jeep driver's own mechanical knowledge, which is generally solid since their vehicles take a beating daily.

Jeep hire: this is genuinely how "local guide" works for most of the remote spots in this document — you hire a jeep with driver in the last accessible

town (Thal, Utror, Sassi, Bilamik, Madaglasht, etc.), and the driver either guides you directly or connects you with a local porter/guide on arrival. There's no separate "book a guide in advance" infrastructure for most of these places outside the big-name treks (K2, Rakaposhi, Fairy Meadows) that the tour operators above run as formal packages.

Cultural festivals worth timing a trip around

Nowruz (Nauroze) — March 21-23, celebrated in Gilgit, Hunza, Skardu, and Chitral: polo, football, volleyball, hockey, folk dances and music.

Chilam Joshi — May, Kalash spring festival in Bumburet/Rumbur/Birir, four days of music and dancing — already noted in Region 7.

Ginani — late June/early July, Hunza and Nagar's wheat-harvest festival: orchards, traditional dress, Shina/Burushaski songs, and harissa (a meat-and- wheat dish).

Shandur Polo Festival — 3,700m, the world's highest polo ground, Gilgit vs. Chitral in a free- flowing traditional format dating to 1936, held July 7-9 — accommodation is tent-camping only, book/plan well ahead. Genuinely one of the most spectacular single events on this whole list if the timing works.

Uchal — August, Kalash harvest festival.

Silk Route Festival — Hunza and Ghizer, celebrating the region's Silk Road heritage with traditional music, crafts, and food.

Choimus — December (winter solstice), Kalash's largest festival — cold-weather trip, but a genuinely different experience of the valleys than the summer trekking season this whole document is otherwise built around.

Two corrections from last time, and two more

just found

Doing the actual research turned up a few places on your list that I'd mentally filed under "Hunza" but that don't actually belong here geographically — flagging so the doc stays accurate rather than forcing them in:

Charkusa Valley (Husha) — actually in the Hushe valley, Ghanche District, near Khaplu — that's Baltistan, not Hunza. I'll cover it properly with K6/K7 Basecamp when we do the Skardu region.

Izmis Lake — actually in Utror Valley, Swat — not Gilgit-Baltistan at all. I'll cover it with the Swat– Kalam–Kumrat region instead.

Tormik Meadows — actually about 60–70km from Skardu city (via Kachura, Gamba Tormik, Pain Tormik) — same general area as "Dunsa Tormik, Skardu" from your list, so these two are almost certainly the same place. Will cover together in the Skardu region.

Hundarap Valley & Khukush Lake — both actually in Ghizer District, not Hunza. A lakes list you shared confirms they're the same place: "Handarap Lake," a high-altitude lake in the Shandur Valley area of Gupis-Yasin District, 3,285m elevation, in Handarap Nallah/Handarap Valley, Tehsil Phander — reached via the KKH from Islamabad to Gilgit, then a 4-hour walk from Handarap Valley

settlement, consistent with what I'd found earlier calling it "Khukush Lake (also called Baha Lake)," the third-largest lake in northern Pakistan by surface area on the Phander–Shandur road. Since it's right next door to Karambar Lake/Ishkoman which I've already covered above, I'm treating it as done rather than deferring it further.

Emergency numbers (work nationwide,

including GB, AJK, and KPK)

Rescue 1122 — ambulance, fire, and rescue; the main one to know, 24/7, works even without phone credit. Now linked with the Pakistan Emergency Helpline (PEHEL)-911 in GB specifically, and GB

Rescue 1122 has a dedicated bike emergency response unit for exactly the kind of travel you do.

Police — 15 Edhi Foundation ambulance — 115 (nationwide, free, largest ambulance network in the country) Fire — 16 Motorway Police — 130 (relevant for the M-1/Swat Motorway/Hazara Expressway stretches) GB Tourist Police Helpline — 1422, or 05811- 930055 — this is the one to call for theft, scams, harassment, disputes with a service provider, or general "I don't know where to go" situations as a traveler specifically, separate from the general police line.

Documents to carry, and checkpoints

Another gap worth naming: this document mentions "carry CNIC" repeatedly for specific LOC-adjacent areas (Neelum, Astore/Minimarg) but never laid out the full picture for a bike trip covering this many regions.

Always carry: original CNIC (not a photo of it — checkpoints in AJK and near the LOC specifically ask for the original), your bike's registration book, and your driving license. KKH, Neelum, and Astore/Deosai routes all have periodic checkpoints where these get checked.

Route-specific paperwork already noted elsewhere in this document: the Minimarg NOC (Region 3), CKNP trekking permits for Hushe-valley treks including K2/K6/K7/Masherbrum (Region 2), and Deosai park entry fees (Region 2) — those are covered at point of use, not repeated here.

Fuel guide — where to refuel, and the long gaps

between pumps

The single biggest practical gap in this whole document until now. On a 125cc bike especially, running out mid-gap isn't a minor inconvenience — some of these stretches have no settlements at all, so plan every fill-up around these gaps rather than assuming "there'll be something eventually."

KKH corridor (Islamabad → Hunza → Khunjerab):

Mansehra has a service station; the next one is at Thakot, about 70km further — fill up in Mansehra even if you're not empty.

Besham (290km from Islamabad) is the last major petrol stop before the mountain gorges begin — top off here regardless of your gauge; the ~210km

stretch to Chilas is remote and slow-going, not a place to be searching for fuel.

Chilas (500km) has a named pump — Gunar Farm Chilas — with the next one at Jaglot.

Gilgit (610km) and Karimabad/Hunza (700km) are both reliable fuel hubs with multiple pumps.

Passu (770km) has limited options — fill up in Karimabad/Aliabad before heading further up- valley if you're continuing toward Sost/Khunjerab.

Sost (810km) is the last Pakistani town before the Khunjerab border and has reliable fuel — this is your last chance before the pass.

Sost → Khunjerab Pass (~75-90km one-way) has no fuel whatsoever — this is a there-and-back stretch from Sost for most riders (day trip up to the pass and back), so fill up completely in Sost before making the run.

Kaghan Valley → Babusar → Chilas:

Fill your tank in Naran — there is no petrol pump after Batakundi (12km past Naran), all the way over Babusar Top and down to Chilas — that's roughly 90-100km with nothing.

This is one of the least forgiving gaps on your whole list precisely because it's also a high pass (4,173m) — don't attempt it on a low tank even if you think you can coast down the Chilas side.

Astore / Deosai / Skardu:

Astore valley entrance has a fuel stop — fill up completely here.

There is no fuel option from Chillam through Deosai all the way to Skardu city — this is a genuinely long, high-altitude gap (100km+) with zero settlements offering fuel. Confirmed by an actual motorbike trip report (Suzuki GS-150), not just a general guide — take it seriously.

Between Skardu and Khaplu, there's only one fuel station, at Ghawari — relevant if you're doing the Khaplu/Hushe leg of Region 2.

Swat/Kalam → Kumrat:

Kalam is the last town with reliable fuel infrastructure. Utror and Thal (the gateway to Kumrat/Jahaz Banda) are both described as small villages with only basic amenities — don't count on fuel past Kalam. Fill up there before heading to Utror, Gabral, Mahodand, or over Badgoi Pass toward Kumrat.

Chitral → Shandur/Booni/Mastuj:

→ Shandur/Booni/Mastuj:

Chitral town and Booni (the Upper Chitral hub) are the reliable fuel points on this corridor. Mastuj, Sor Laspur, and the Shandur Pass area itself are small settlements with thin infrastructure — fill up fully at Booni before continuing toward Shandur or into the Yarkhun/Broghil direction.

Neelum Valley:

Muzaffarabad is the main hub. Athmuqam and Kel have basic bazaars and likely fuel, but Taobat (the last village in the valley) and the jeep tracks off the main road (toward Ratti Gali, Arang Kel, Chitta Katta) don't — fill up in Athmuqam or Kel before pushing further up-valley.

The general pattern across every remote jeep-track valley on this list (Chapursan, Shimshal, Naltar, Bilamik/Thorsay, Madaglasht, Hushe): fuel exists in the last KKH/main-road town before the turnoff (Sost for Chapursan, Karimabad/Shishkat area for Shimshal, Nomal for Naltar, the Skardu-road towns for Bilamik, Chitral town for Madaglasht, Khaplu for Hushe) and nowhere beyond it. REGION 2: Skardu–Baltistan

Getting there from Islamabad/Rawalpindi

By air: PIA, Airblue, and AirSial all fly Islamabad → Skardu (KDU) direct, about 1–1h10m in the air, roughly 24 weekly departures between them. Fares run roughly PKR 12,000–45,000 one-way depending on timing and season — book early, this route sells out fast in peak season (Eid, summer holidays). Flights are almost always morning departures since mountain visibility is best early, and weather cancellations are common — don't book it on a tight schedule.

By bike: The road distance is roughly 630–700 km, taking 12–14 hours of actual driving depending on route and conditions — realistically 2 days on a 125cc. Route: Islamabad → Hazara Motorway → Mansehra → Besham → Dasu → Chilas → Jaglot → turn off the

KKH onto the Skardu Road (S-1) → Skardu. The Skardu Road was rebuilt by FWO and is now mostly paved and smooth — noticeably better surface than parts of the KKH itself. Same fuel-stop logic as the Hunza run: fill up at every town, nothing reliable on the Jaglot–Skardu stretch.

By local bus: NATCO runs Islamabad/Rawalpindi → Skardu directly, fares around PKR 4,630–5,500 depending on bus class, with buses departing daily around 2pm and the trip taking the same 12–14 hours as the drive.

Skardu city — getting settled

Hotels: Range widely — popular mid-range options run roughly PKR 14,000–30,800/night, with luxury lakeside resorts near Kachura going up to PKR 67,750+. Budget guesthouses exist in Skardu city center at lower rates than this, though exact figures are harder to pin down online — worth checking on arrival or via Bookme.

What's in the city itself: Kharpocho Fort ("King of Forts," built late 17th century by Ali Sher Khan Anchan) overlooks the city and the confluence of the Indus and Shigar rivers, the Katpana Cold Desert (also called Biama Nakpo), Upper and Lower Kachura Lakes (Lower Kachura = Shangrila, with its famous red-roof resort), and Satpara Lake

(a dammed lake, built by Ali Sher Khan Anchan in the 1580s–1624).

Food: Balti cuisine leans on wheat, buckwheat, dried apricots and yak/beef rather than rice. Worth trying: Prapu (hand-made wheat noodles in a ground-walnut-and-apricot-oil sauce), Balay (a family of soups — Traspi Balay is the most notable), Mamtu (steamed dumplings, same as Hunza), and fresh trout — several fish farms around Kharmang and Khaplu serve it straight from the stream.

The old pass sits at 3,118m and is only usable in summer — some jeep operators and locals still cross it directly (a rough but scenic alternative) when the tunnel is congested or for the views themselves, July-September only. The tunnel is now the default for anyone not specifically chasing the pass-crossing experience.

Lowari Top: A winter snowfall viewpoint about 5 hours from Islamabad, with Kalash about 2 hours further and Chitral about 3 hours further from there — a genuine standalone winter day-trip destination in its own right, separate from just transiting through.

Chitrali food

Genuinely distinct from anything else on this list — worth a dedicated stop even outside of any specific trek.

Shorba — slow-cooked lamb/goat bone broth with dried tomato and wild herbs, the valley's

foundational dish, eaten at everything from weddings to ordinary dinners.

Chapshuro/Chapshoro — the "Chitrali pizza," a flatbread stuffed with spiced minced meat, onion, coriander, and chili, cooked on a griddle; each valley has its own variation, some adding wild leeks or dried apricot — this is a standard trail food, especially at Shandur during the polo festival.

Ghalmandi — layered flatbread with cottage cheese, coriander, chives, and walnut oil; Cheera Shapik is the same idea with a béchamel-style white sauce instead of cheese.

Dudo pati — loose-leaf tea simmered directly in whole milk, sometimes with salt and dried apricot; also served as salty butter tea. Genuinely warming at 3,000m — worth trying once even if it sounds odd.

Also look for: Chitrali maash daal cooked in walnut oil, organic honey and mantu/mantoo dumplings, and Chitral town's food street for chapli kebab if you want something more familiar.

Nanga Parbat Base Camp — Rupal Face

(Astore/Tarashing side)

Route: Astore → Tarashing village (~30km, 2 hours by rough unpaved jeep road, last village in Rupal Valley) → trek in via the Tarashing Glacier's lateral moraine → Rupal village → Herligkoffer Base Camp (also called Rupal Base Camp, named after German mountaineer Karl Herligkoffer).

Distance/elevation: About 26-30km round trip from Tarashing, 3-4 days, reaching Herligkoffer Base Camp at ~3,500-3,550m — Tarashing itself sits at 2,900-2,911m.

What you're looking at: The Rupal Face rises 4,600m from the valley floor to the summit — the single greatest vertical rise of any mountain face on Earth.

Difficulty: Moderate — easy trails with two short, non-technical glacier crossings, genuinely less crowded than the Fairy Meadows side despite being just as dramatic.

Extension option: trekkers can continue past base camp to Shaigiri (5,584m) or all the way to Mazeno Base Camp / Mazeno La (~5,400m) for those wanting to push further — this would push the trip from "moderate" into genuinely serious high- altitude territory.

Practical notes: No phone signal on the trail, camping only (no guesthouses past Tarashing), a guide is recommended especially for a first Pakistan trek, porters are hired locally from Tarashing and Chorit villages.

Combining both sides: several operators run Fairy Meadows and Rupal Face as one connected trip (Tarashing → Rupal side → back to Astore → over to Raikot Bridge → Fairy Meadows side), which is worth considering if you're making the long trip out to this region anyway rather than doing two separate trips.

Chilinji Pass

What it is: A high mountain pass at 5,335m connecting the Karambar valley in Ishkoman (Ghizer District) with the Chapursan valley in Upper Hunza — this is the direct link between the two remote areas already covered above.

Route: Most commonly crossed from the Chapursan side, though the ascent from that direction is notably steeper and more technical (crevasses, scree) than approaching from Ishkoman.

Difficulty: Genuinely serious — porters in Ishkoman have refused to attempt it before, citing the difficulty. Not a beginner or even intermediate trek.

Bigger picture: Chilinji is usually done as part of a longer traverse — a full Wakhan-corridor-adjacent route crosses Darkot (4,575m), Karambar (4,320m), and Chilinji (5,291m) passes in sequence, connecting Chitral to Chapursan and Hunza. If you're already planning Karambar Lake, this could extend into a much bigger multi-week route rather than a there-and-back trip.

Season: June–August strictly — this is not a shoulder-season objective.

Batura Glacier Trek (Yashpirt/"Yashperth")

What it is: the trek you had listed as "Yashperth" is Yashpirt — a beautiful high meadow with shepherd huts at around 3,400–3,630m, with views of the Batura peaks, the Batura icefall, and Distaghil Sar (7,885m). Route: Borith Lake → Yunzben (11.5km, 6–7 hrs) → across the Batura Glacier → Yashpirt (5.7km, 6– 7 hrs). The Batura Glacier itself is around 57–65km long — one of the longest outside the polar regions.

Difficulty: Challenging but non-technical — a genuine alternative to Baltoro/Concordia for people who want raw wilderness without needing mountaineering skills.

On "Sheerin Maidon Lake": I couldn't independently confirm a lake by this exact name. A related bonus find from a lakes list you shared: "Batura Lake" is a real, named lake right at the edge of the Batura Glacier, visible from the KKH after Passu village, around 2,900m — this may or may not be the same lake as "Sheerin Maidon," but it's a confirmed, named feature on this exact route worth knowing about either way. Still worth confirming the exact spot with a guide in Passu or Gulmit.

Season: May–September.

Fuel guide — where to refuel, and the long gaps

between pumps

The single biggest practical gap in this whole document until now. On a 125cc bike especially, running out mid-gap isn't a minor inconvenience — some of these stretches have no settlements at all, so plan every fill-up around these gaps rather than assuming "there'll be something eventually."

KKH corridor (Islamabad → Hunza → Khunjerab):

Mansehra has a service station; the next one is at Thakot, about 70km further — fill up in Mansehra even if you're not empty.

Besham (290km from Islamabad) is the last major petrol stop before the mountain gorges begin — top off here regardless of your gauge; the ~210km

stretch to Chilas is remote and slow-going, not a place to be searching for fuel.

Chilas (500km) has a named pump — Gunar Farm Chilas — with the next one at Jaglot.

Gilgit (610km) and Karimabad/Hunza (700km) are both reliable fuel hubs with multiple pumps.

Passu (770km) has limited options — fill up in Karimabad/Aliabad before heading further up- valley if you're continuing toward Sost/Khunjerab.

Sost (810km) is the last Pakistani town before the Khunjerab border and has reliable fuel — this is your last chance before the pass.

Sost → Khunjerab Pass (~75-90km one-way) has no fuel whatsoever — this is a there-and-back stretch from Sost for most riders (day trip up to the pass and back), so fill up completely in Sost before making the run.

Kaghan Valley → Babusar → Chilas:

Fill your tank in Naran — there is no petrol pump after Batakundi (12km past Naran), all the way over Babusar Top and down to Chilas — that's roughly 90-100km with nothing.

This is one of the least forgiving gaps on your whole list precisely because it's also a high pass (4,173m) — don't attempt it on a low tank even if you think you can coast down the Chilas side.

Astore / Deosai / Skardu:

Astore valley entrance has a fuel stop — fill up completely here.

There is no fuel option from Chillam through Deosai all the way to Skardu city — this is a genuinely long, high-altitude gap (100km+) with zero settlements offering fuel. Confirmed by an actual motorbike trip report (Suzuki GS-150), not just a general guide — take it seriously.

Between Skardu and Khaplu, there's only one fuel station, at Ghawari — relevant if you're doing the Khaplu/Hushe leg of Region 2.

Swat/Kalam → Kumrat:

Kalam is the last town with reliable fuel infrastructure. Utror and Thal (the gateway to Kumrat/Jahaz Banda) are both described as small villages with only basic amenities — don't count on fuel past Kalam. Fill up there before heading to Utror, Gabral, Mahodand, or over Badgoi Pass toward Kumrat.

Chitral → Shandur/Booni/Mastuj:

— December (winter solstice), Kalash's largest festival — cold-weather trip, but a genuinely different experience of the valleys than the summer trekking season this whole document is otherwise built around.

Kharmang-Shigar Polo Festival, Babusar Polo Festival, Jashn-e-Hunar — smaller regional polo/craft festivals mentioned across sources but with less consistent date information; worth asking locally or checking with Visit GB closer to your travel dates if timing matters.

REGION 1: Hunza–Nagar–Gojal

Corridor

Getting there from Islamabad/Rawalpindi

By bike: ~600–650 km on the Karakoram Highway (N- 35). Two options:

Year-round route: Islamabad → Hazara Motorway → Mansehra → Besham → Dasu (Kohistan) → Chilas → Gilgit → Hunza. This is the only option outside summer.

Naran–Babusar route (May–Oct only): Islamabad → Mansehra → Balakot → Naran → Babusar Top (4,173m) → Chilas → Gilgit → Hunza. Shorter and far more scenic, but Babusar closes with the first snow, and it's a serious high-altitude pass on a 125cc — go in daylight, watch fuel.

Realistic riding time: 14–20 hours of actual road time. Nobody sane does this in one day on a bike — plan 2 days with an overnight in Besham/Chilas/Naran, or 3 if you want to actually enjoy it.

Fuel stops: Mansehra, Besham, Chilas, Gilgit all have pumps; nothing reliable in between on the KKH stretch, so fill up at every town.

The KKH has been largely improved under CPEC, but sections after Chilas can still be narrow and winding.

By local bus: NATCO (government-run, Northern Areas Transport Corporation) is the main operator, with Faisal Movers and Silk Route also running the route now.

Islamabad/Rawalpindi → Gilgit: PKR 3,760; Islamabad/Rawalpindi → Hunza: PKR 5,040. Fares have crept up through 2026 — some listings now show PKR 5,500+ on the AC Yutong buses.

Travel time is around 13–14 hours on the newer express services, though 16–20 hours is more typical with rest stops.

Faisal Movers specifically (you asked about this one): runs Islamabad → Hunza directly, PKR 4,500–5,000 depending on class. Departure from Pirwadhai Crystal Lines Terminal in Islamabad/Rawalpindi (or the "26-number" terminal) — book ahead in peak season, seats sell out. Their Gilgit-end terminal is on Shahr-e-Quaid-e- Azam, near the NATCO terminal, opposite Skyways — contact 0311-1224488 for booking/timing queries. Return departures from Gilgit run between 12:00pm and 8:00pm.

From Gilgit onward to Karimabad: frequent shared vans/Hiace/Suzuki wagons, roughly 2 hours, cheap (a few hundred PKR).

If you ever need a second/backup bike here: rental shops cluster around Jutial in Gilgit and Aliabad in Hunza — see the Practical Reference Guide at the top of this document for named operators (Pakistan Bikers, AMT Expeditions) and rates.

K2 Base Camp & Gondogoro La (GGLA)

Route: Skardu → jeep to Askole (last village, ~7 hours), then on foot: Jhola → Paiju (rest day) →

Khoburtse → Urdukas → Goro II → Concordia → K2 Base Camp, then either return the same way or cross Gondogoro La (5,585m) down into Hushe Valley.

Distance/days: About 160km total, 12–14 days of trekking plus 4+ days of transport — most full packages run 18–22 days Islamabad to Islamabad.

Elevation: K2 Base Camp itself sits around 5,000m; Gondogoro La is the high point at 5,585m.

Gear/guide: A guide, porter, and CKNP permit are mandatory; crossing Gondogoro La needs crampons, a climbing harness, and a carabiner, with fixed ropes available July–August for a fee (~PKR 28,000 for up to 2 people).

Cost: Getting the letter-of-invitation visa support plus CKNP fee runs about $900 (roughly PKR 250,000), guide+porter+their food roughly separate, and jeep transport in/out about $1,100 (roughly PKR 306,000) — this is genuinely one of the most expensive treks on your whole list, before even counting the guided-package markup.

This is the big one. If you only do one "expedition- grade" trek off this entire 100+ place list, this is the one most people mean when they say it.

Shigar Valley

Shigar town: About 45km / 40–50 min drive from Skardu, on the way to Askole. Home to the 17th-

century Shigar Fort — now a Serena heritage hotel — and the 14th-century Amburiq Mosque.

Arandu Valley & Chogo Lungma Glacier ice caves: About 4 hours by jeep further up-valley from Skardu, in upper Shigar District. This is the "Aroundu Glacier" from your list — ice caves carved into the 44km Chogo Lungma Glacier, best visited December–February when the ice is most stable, and also the Baltistan-side approach route to Spantik/Golden Peak covered back in Region 1.

Snow Lake & Hispar La Trek

What it is: A 16km-wide glacial basin at 4,800m where the Biafo and Hispar glaciers meet, connecting Hunza (west) to Baltistan (east) via the Hispar La pass — this is genuinely a cross-region expedition, not a Hunza-only trek.

Two directions: Most groups start from Askole (Skardu side) and finish in Hispar village (Hunza/Nagar side), or occasionally the reverse.

Distance/duration: About 190 km total, 12 days classic itinerary, though full trips including travel run around 3 weeks door to door, with 12 days of high-altitude trekking.

Elevation: Hispar Pass tops out at 5,150m. Difficulty: Strenuous, remote, requires a certified guide and full camping/porter support — no shortcuts here, and no bike or bus gets anywhere near it.

Season: June–September only.

Note for later: we'll cover the Skardu-side approach (Askole, Baltoro) properly when we get to Region 2.

Chapursan Valley & Baldiyat Meadows

Route: KKH to Sost (last town before Khunjerab) → turn off onto the Chapursan valley road → Zood Khun (last village).

Distance/time: About a 4-hour jeep ride from Sost to Zood Khun; roughly 6 hours total from Karimabad, 8 from Gilgit. The Sost–Chapursan road is narrow and rough — not one to underestimate on a loaded bike; go slow and consider it jeep territory past the first villages.

Local transport: One public jeep a day runs the valley, leaving Zood Khun around 5:30–6am — good to know if you're not self-driving.

What's there: Baba Ghundi Shrine (2 hrs beyond Zood Khun), Yishkok Meadow (base for treks toward Yashkuk Yaz Glacier and Sakar Sar base camp, the valley's highest peak at 6,272m), and several scattered Wakhi villages.

Accommodation: Guesthouses and homestays in Zood Khun and nearby villages — basic but authentic Wakhi hospitality.

Best time: June–August, when meadows are in bloom and trails are most accessible. Expect no reliable signal or WiFi once you're past Sost — worth knowing if you're planning to vlog live.

Culture note: If your timing lines up (June– September), Kyrgyz traders sometimes cross from Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor via the Irshad Pass to trade at Chapursan — and there's an annual two-

day Baba Ghundi Festival with traditional games like buzkashi.

Astore town & Rama Meadows/Lake

What's there: Astore itself sits at about 2,600m (8,500ft), 60km from Gilgit, serving mainly as a jumping-off base. Rama Meadows/Lake is about 10-13km from Astore, roughly 1h40 by jeep on a rough 4x4-only road — a popular easy add-on for camping and stargazing, not on your original list by name but effectively part of the same trip since it's this close to Astore.

Local transport within the valley: Astore to Tarashing (the Rupal Face trailhead) runs about PKR 50 shared / PKR 1,000 special hire, roughly 2 hours.

Food: Astore shares Gilgit-Baltistan's broader food culture already covered in Regions 1 and 2 (apricot dishes, Mamtu dumplings, trout) rather than having its own distinct cuisine — nothing new to add here beyond what's already in those sections.

Fairy Meadows & Nanga Parbat Base Camp

(Raikot/north side)

Route: Islamabad → Raikot Bridge on the KKH (~540km, 10-12 hours) → 4x4 jeep from Raikot Bridge to Tattu village (15-16km, 90-120 min on a narrow single-lane track, PKR 12,000-15,000 per jeep for up to 6 people) → trek 3-5.5km on foot (2- 3 hours) to Fairy Meadows.

This jeep track is genuinely not bike territory — narrow, one-lane, and normally driven only by experienced local jeep drivers; leave the bike at Raikot Bridge or Chilas and go in by the local jeep service.

Elevation/onward trek: Fairy Meadows sits at ~3,300m. From there: Beyal Camp is a 3km/4-5 hour return hike, then optionally on to Nanga Parbat Base Camp itself with views of the Rupal Face — "the largest mountain face on earth" — from Reflection Point along the way.

Cost: A complete 2-night trip from Islamabad runs roughly $300-480/person in 2026 (roughly PKR 83,000-133,000); organized multi-day packages

with hotel/camping run PKR 24,600-54,600, or up to $850-990 (roughly PKR 236,000-275,000) for the fuller guided versions. Cabin stays at places like Broad View Hotel run about $60/person twin-share with breakfast and dinner (roughly PKR 16,700).

Season: Mid-June to mid-September is most reliable for both the jeep track being open and Nanga Parbat actually being visible. Difficulty: Moderate — this is genuinely one of the more accessible "big mountain" experiences in the entire country, which is exactly why it's so popular.

Kumrat Valley, Jahaz Banda & Katora Lake —

resolving the visited-list question

Good news: these turn out to be the same trek, not two separate lakes — so nothing to untangle. Katora Lake is reached via Jahaz Banda Meadows; Jahaz Banda is the overnight stop and Katora Lake is the destination beyond it, in the upper reaches of Kumrat Valley, Upper Dir District.

Route: Islamabad → Swat Motorway to Chakdara → N-45 through Timergara and Dir → Thal (last town for normal vehicles), ~370-460km, 8-10 hours → jeep from Thal to Taki/Takki Banda, 16km rough track, ~1.5 hours, PKR 5,000 one-way or PKR 10,000-12,000 round trip with overnight → trek 3-5 hours to Jahaz Banda Meadows (camping) → further 3-4 hours to Katora Lake.

Alternative approach from Kalam (Swat side): via Utror → Badgoi Pass → Taki Top, about 3-4 hours, then the same trek onward — genuinely a second valid way in if you're already based in Kalam rather than coming fresh from Islamabad.

Katora Lake: ~3,500m elevation, bowl-shaped (that's what "Katora" means in Pashto), with a smaller "Chota Katora"/Jahaz Banda Lake and a black-stoned spring called Kala Chashma along the way.

Kumrat Waterfall: About 12-13km from Thal, jeep- accessible, requires a short hike to actually see it since it's not visible from the road.

Practical note: no electricity or real food options at Katora Lake itself — carry supplies, and bring a power bank and flashlight. This is genuinely remote-feeling despite being a well-known name.

→ Shandur/Booni/Mastuj:

Muzaffarabad is the main hub. Athmuqam and Kel have basic bazaars and likely fuel, but Taobat (the last village in the valley) and the jeep tracks off the main road (toward Ratti Gali, Arang Kel, Chitta Katta) don't — fill up in Athmuqam or Kel before pushing further up-valley.

Connectivity, cash, and seasonal road closures

SIM/network: SCOM is Gilgit-Baltistan's own network and generally has the best coverage in- region — already noted for Neelum specifically but worth knowing as a general rule across GB, not just AJK. Major national networks (Jazz, Zong, Telenor, Ufone) have patchy coverage once you're off the KKH/main roads, and several specific spots in this document (Chapursan, Hushe past Saicho, most

multi-day treks) have no signal at all — that's noted at point of use throughout.

Cash: ATMs exist in Gilgit, Skardu, Hunza (Karimabad/Aliabad), Chitral town, and Mingora — not much beyond that. Carry enough cash for each region's leg before heading into the valleys; jeep hire, guesthouses, and local guides are almost entirely cash transactions.

Seasonal closures, consolidated: Babusar Pass (Kaghan-to-Gilgit link) closes with first winter snow, reopens ~May; Shandur Pass (Chitral-to-Gilgit link) is summer-only; Deosai's road closes to vehicles roughly November-May; Lowari is now tunneled year-round so less of a concern than it used to be, though the old pass itself is still summer-only for those specifically chasing that route. Most individual trek season windows (May/June- September) are already noted per entry — this is just the connecting-road picture.

Shah Jinali Pass & Thui Pass (moved from

What it is: A combined trek in the Hindu Raj range crossing from Upper Chitral into Gilgit-Baltistan — Shah Jinali Pass (called "the King's Polo Ground" locally, 4,259m) connects Rich Gol/Turikho valley with Yarkhun, and Thui Pass (4,499m-4,500m) continues on from Yarkhun into the Yasin Valley, Ghizer District. Connects Shigar Valley to Khaplu/Hushe area, running along the Central Karakoram National Park boundary. The zone is still militarized and NOC-gated regardless of vehicle: get the NOC from the Assistant Commissioner's office at the start of Rama Road near the Astore lorry depot — bring your bike/car number and CNIC, they'll type and stamp three copies on the spot, then hand copies over at the Army Mess checkpoint on Deosai Road. If you ride the YBR out there, plan to leave it in Astore and go the last stretch by jeep or a rented/borrowed 150cc+ bike.

Rainbow Lake, resolved: this is actually inside Minimarg itself, not a separate Astore-area stop —

an artificial lake built by the Army near Domail/Domel, about 12km past the Minimarg checkpost, known for turquoise water and photogenic surroundings, with nearby Crystal Lake as a bonus stop. So the same 150cc+ rule above applies to reaching it.

REGION 2: Skardu–Baltistan

Getting there from Islamabad/Rawalpindi

By air: PIA, Airblue, and AirSial all fly Islamabad → Skardu (KDU) direct, about 1–1h10m in the air, roughly 24 weekly departures between them. Fares run roughly PKR 12,000–45,000 one-way depending on timing and season — book early, this route sells out fast in peak season (Eid, summer holidays). Flights are almost always morning departures since mountain visibility is best early, and weather cancellations are common — don't book it on a tight schedule.

By bike: The road distance is roughly 630–700 km, taking 12–14 hours of actual driving depending on route and conditions — realistically 2 days on a 125cc. Route: Islamabad → Hazara Motorway → Mansehra → Besham → Dasu → Chilas → Jaglot → turn off the

KKH onto the Skardu Road (S-1) → Skardu. The Skardu Road was rebuilt by FWO and is now mostly paved and smooth — noticeably better surface than parts of the KKH itself. Same fuel-stop logic as the Hunza run: fill up at every town, nothing reliable on the Jaglot–Skardu stretch.

By local bus: NATCO runs Islamabad/Rawalpindi → Skardu directly, fares around PKR 4,630–5,500 depending on bus class, with buses departing daily around 2pm and the trip taking the same 12–14 hours as the drive.

Skardu city — getting settled

Hotels: Range widely — popular mid-range options run roughly PKR 14,000–30,800/night, with luxury lakeside resorts near Kachura going up to PKR 67,750+. Budget guesthouses exist in Skardu city center at lower rates than this, though exact figures are harder to pin down online — worth checking on arrival or via Bookme.

What's in the city itself: Kharpocho Fort ("King of Forts," built late 17th century by Ali Sher Khan Anchan) overlooks the city and the confluence of the Indus and Shigar rivers, the Katpana Cold Desert (also called Biama Nakpo), Upper and Lower Kachura Lakes (Lower Kachura = Shangrila, with its famous red-roof resort), and Satpara Lake

(a dammed lake, built by Ali Sher Khan Anchan in the 1580s–1624).

Worth trying: Prapu (hand-made wheat noodles in a ground-walnut-and-apricot-oil sauce), Balay (a family of soups — Traspi Balay is the most notable), Mamtu (steamed dumplings, same as Hunza), and fresh trout — several fish farms around Kharmang and Khaplu serve it straight from the stream.

Shimshal Pass & Minglik Sar

Start point: Shimshal Valley — reached by a jeep road (the famous Shimshal jeep track) branching off the KKH near Passu, running through Attabad Lake, Gulmit, and Hussaini. This road can be covered by jeep in a day from Hunza — rough enough that most operators use jeeps rather than bikes for it, though it's technically driveable on a light bike in good weather.

What it is: Shimshal Valley (3,000m) is the highest permanent settlement in Hunza, home to about 2,240 households, and the historic gateway used by Hunza raiders on China-India trade routes. Route: Shimshal Village → Korband → Gharsar → Peryan Sar → Shujerab → Shimshal Pass (4,735m) → onward to the Shimshal Lakes and Minglik Sar base camp.

Minglik Sar: A 6,050m peak in the Pamir sub-range — the 31st highest peak in the world by some rankings — requiring genuine mountaineering skill for the summit, not just trekking fitness.

Days: A full trek-plus-climb itinerary runs 16–22 days from Islamabad; the trek to Shimshal Pass alone (without summiting Minglik Sar) is

considerably shorter but still a serious multi-day commitment.

Difficulty: Challenging — high-altitude terrain, steep ascents, glacial crossings; prior trekking experience recommended, though fit beginners can manage with proper acclimatization.

Season: June–September.

Note: This is genuinely one of the more remote treks on your whole list — Shimshal only got a jeep road in the early 2000s, and the valley's isolation is a big part of why it's still this untouched.

Golden Peak (Spantik)

What it is: Also called Spantik or "Ghenish Chhish" (Golden Mountain in Brushaski) — the northwest face glows gold at sunset when viewed from Nagar/Karimabad, which is where the name comes from. It sits east of Diran and northeast of Malubiting.

Elevation: 7,027m — one of the most attainable 7,000m peaks in the Karakoram, often used as a stepping-stone climb before attempting 8,000m peaks.

Access: Two approaches exist — from Arandu village in Shigar District (Baltistan side) and from Hopar Valley in Nagar District (Hunza side). The Nagar-side approach is the one that fits this region.

Base camp: Reached via 3 days trekking on the Chogolungma Glacier, base camp sits at 4,100m.

Difficulty: Graded AD (technical), requiring prior high-altitude mountaineering experience — this is a real climb, not a trek. Previous 6,000m experience is strongly recommended.

Season: June–August.

Realistic framing: this belongs on a "someday, after building up 6,000m experience" list rather than a near-term trip — but the base camp trek portion alone is a legitimate (if very committing) objective on its own.

Correction — Minimarg bike rules: My earlier note that motorbikes aren't permitted was wrong. The actual rule: minimum 150cc bikes are allowed into Minimarg — it's bikes under 150cc and regular cars that get turned away; you need either a 4x4 jeep or a 150cc+ bike. If you ride the YBR out there, plan to leave it in Astore and go the last stretch by jeep or a rented/borrowed 150cc+ bike.
