Fairy Meadows & Nanga Parbat Base Camp

(Raikot/north side)

Route: Islamabad → Raikot Bridge on the KKH (~540km, 10-12 hours) → 4x4 jeep from Raikot Bridge to Tattu village (15-16km, 90-120 min on a narrow single-lane track, PKR 12,000-15,000 per jeep for up to 6 people) → trek 3-5.5km on foot (2- 3 hours) to Fairy Meadows.

This jeep track is genuinely not bike territory — narrow, one-lane, and normally driven only by experienced local jeep drivers; leave the bike at Raikot Bridge or Chilas and go in by the local jeep service.

Elevation/onward trek: Fairy Meadows sits at ~3,300m. From there: Beyal Camp is a 3km/4-5 hour return hike, then optionally on to Nanga Parbat Base Camp itself with views of the Rupal Face — "the largest mountain face on earth" — from Reflection Point along the way.

Cost: A complete 2-night trip from Islamabad runs roughly $300-480/person in 2026 (roughly PKR 83,000-133,000); organized multi-day packages

with hotel/camping run PKR 24,600-54,600, or up to $850-990 (roughly PKR 236,000-275,000) for the fuller guided versions. Cabin stays at places like Broad View Hotel run about $60/person twin-share with breakfast and dinner (roughly PKR 16,700).

Season: Mid-June to mid-September is most reliable for both the jeep track being open and Nanga Parbat actually being visible. Difficulty: Moderate — this is genuinely one of the more accessible "big mountain" experiences in the entire country, which is exactly why it's so popular.

Shimshal Pass & Minglik Sar

Start point: Shimshal Valley — reached by a jeep road (the famous Shimshal jeep track) branching off the KKH near Passu, running through Attabad Lake, Gulmit, and Hussaini. This road can be covered by jeep in a day from Hunza — rough enough that most operators use jeeps rather than bikes for it, though it's technically driveable on a light bike in good weather.

What it is: Shimshal Valley (3,000m) is the highest permanent settlement in Hunza, home to about 2,240 households, and the historic gateway used by Hunza raiders on China-India trade routes. Route: Shimshal Village → Korband → Gharsar → Peryan Sar → Shujerab → Shimshal Pass (4,735m) → onward to the Shimshal Lakes and Minglik Sar base camp.

Minglik Sar: A 6,050m peak in the Pamir sub-range — the 31st highest peak in the world by some rankings — requiring genuine mountaineering skill for the summit, not just trekking fitness.

Days: A full trek-plus-climb itinerary runs 16–22 days from Islamabad; the trek to Shimshal Pass alone (without summiting Minglik Sar) is

considerably shorter but still a serious multi-day commitment.

Difficulty: Challenging — high-altitude terrain, steep ascents, glacial crossings; prior trekking experience recommended, though fit beginners can manage with proper acclimatization.

Season: June–September.

Note: This is genuinely one of the more remote treks on your whole list — Shimshal only got a jeep road in the early 2000s, and the valley's isolation is a big part of why it's still this untouched.

Golden Peak (Spantik)

What it is: Also called Spantik or "Ghenish Chhish" (Golden Mountain in Brushaski) — the northwest face glows gold at sunset when viewed from Nagar/Karimabad, which is where the name comes from. It sits east of Diran and northeast of Malubiting.

Elevation: 7,027m — one of the most attainable 7,000m peaks in the Karakoram, often used as a stepping-stone climb before attempting 8,000m peaks.

Access: Two approaches exist — from Arandu village in Shigar District (Baltistan side) and from Hopar Valley in Nagar District (Hunza side). The Nagar-side approach is the one that fits this region.

Base camp: Reached via 3 days trekking on the Chogolungma Glacier, base camp sits at 4,100m.

Difficulty: Graded AD (technical), requiring prior high-altitude mountaineering experience — this is a real climb, not a trek. Previous 6,000m experience is strongly recommended.

Season: June–August.

Realistic framing: this belongs on a "someday, after building up 6,000m experience" list rather than a near-term trip — but the base camp trek portion alone is a legitimate (if very committing) objective on its own.

Buskochi (Baskochi) Top

Start point: Shishkat village (near Attabad Lake) — bike-accessible.

Route: A 3–4 hour round trip through light forest and traditional Gojal farmland, up to panoramic views of Attabad Lake and the surrounding villages. Difficulty: Easy — a "hidden gem for those who love nature without the burn," good for a late start, sunset trek, or mellow day with local guides.

Good fit for: a half-day add-on if you're already based near Attabad/Hunza and want a viewpoint hike without committing to a full trek day.

Turgil Meadows (Naltar)

What it is: A meadow high in upper Naltar with views of Rakaposhi and Diran in the distance, about a 2-hour trek from upper Naltar.

Geography note: Naltar Valley is technically reached via Nomal (off the KKH before Hunza proper) and administratively sits closer to Gilgit district than Hunza — I'm covering it here since you already know Naltar from your Sheesha Lake visit, but I'll give it fuller treatment (Naltar Lakes/Bashkiri/Satrangi, the ski resort, Naltar- Pakora trek) alongside Kohistan/Gilgit-corridor spots in a later region.

Kho Nagar Valley (Miacher Kho Meadows) —

added after correcting an earlier misplacement

What it is: "Kho Nagar Valley" from your original list is Miacher Kho Meadows (also just called Kho Meadows), a meadow above Miacher village in Nagar Valley — genuinely in Region 1's territory, not Kohistan as I'd first guessed while researching Region 4. Route: Gilgit → Nagar → Minapin → Miacher village → Kho Meadows, about 3-4 hours total from Gilgit City. A short ~30 minute walk from the parking area up to the meadow itself.

Bike note: Explicitly bike-friendly — the source guide's only caution is to tie down luggage tightly given the road condition, unlike most of the harder- to-reach spots in this region. Good road from the KKH turnoff.

What's there: Views toward Diran Peak, Rakaposhi, Hunza's Duikar viewpoint, Hapakun Meadows, and Rakaposhi Base Camp — essentially a lower-effort viewpoint over the same peaks Rakaposhi Base Camp trekkers work much harder to see. Good fit for: an easy day trip if you're already in Minapin for Rakaposhi Base Camp and want a lighter add-on, or a standalone half-day out of Gilgit/Nagar.

Swat/Kalam/Malam Jabba/Palogha (already visited — hub notes for what follows)

Kalam is the practical base for almost everything north of it — Utror, Gabral, Matiltan, Mahodand Lake, and the jeep hire point for most of the lakes below. Jeep hire in the area generally runs PKR 3,000-5,000 for a half- day/single destination, up to PKR 10,000-12,000 for longer trips like Mahodand, and budget hotel doubles run roughly PKR 800-1,000 in Mingora, PKR 3,000- 5,000 in Kalam itself.

Kumrat Valley, Jahaz Banda & Katora Lake —

resolving the visited-list question

Good news: these turn out to be the same trek, not two separate lakes — so nothing to untangle. Katora Lake is reached via Jahaz Banda Meadows; Jahaz Banda is the overnight stop and Katora Lake is the destination beyond it, in the upper reaches of Kumrat Valley, Upper Dir District.

Route: Islamabad → Swat Motorway to Chakdara → N-45 through Timergara and Dir → Thal (last town for normal vehicles), ~370-460km, 8-10 hours → jeep from Thal to Taki/Takki Banda, 16km rough track, ~1.5 hours, PKR 5,000 one-way or PKR 10,000-12,000 round trip with overnight → trek 3-5 hours to Jahaz Banda Meadows (camping) → further 3-4 hours to Katora Lake.

Alternative approach from Kalam (Swat side): via Utror → Badgoi Pass → Taki Top, about 3-4 hours, then the same trek onward — genuinely a second valid way in if you're already based in Kalam rather than coming fresh from Islamabad.

Katora Lake: ~3,500m elevation, bowl-shaped (that's what "Katora" means in Pashto), with a smaller "Chota Katora"/Jahaz Banda Lake and a black-stoned spring called Kala Chashma along the way.

Kumrat Waterfall: About 12-13km from Thal, jeep- accessible, requires a short hike to actually see it since it's not visible from the road.

Practical note: no electricity or real food options at Katora Lake itself — carry supplies, and bring a power bank and flashlight. This is genuinely remote-feeling despite being a well-known name.

Mastij Lake & Jag Banda (Kalam/Anakar area)

Mastij Lake: 13,081ft, above Janshai Meadows in Anakar Valley, Kalam — long, steep trek through forest and meadow, genuinely demanding per multiple trekker accounts; guide and full camping gear recommended.

Jag Banda: Starts right from Kalam itself — no separate transport needed. Walk from the bridge behind Kalam bazaar to Buyon village (1.5-2 hours) on a paved road, then continue trekking into the higher meadows beyond. One of the more accessible entries in this whole region since it starts in town.

Sheitan Gawt Lake & Sarbanda Lake (deferred from Region 3 — Bahrain/Kedam side)

Sarbanda Lake: In Bahrain, described as the gateway to Sheitan Gawt Lake — a waypoint/meadow stop rather than a final destination in its own right.

Sheitan Gawt (Shaitan Gwat) Lake: Considered the largest lake in Swat, 13,500ft, in alpine pastures above Kedam village near Bahrain. A genuinely long trek — 12-15 hours depending on pace, no guesthouses en route so camping is mandatory, and locals in Kedam itself weren't always well- informed on the route when one trekking blog visited — this is a genuinely under-visited lake even by Swat's already-remote standards. Route in starts via Kedam, just past Bahrain on the Kalam road.

Gabin Jaba, Daral Lake & Chukail Banda (Lower

Swat)

Route: Mingora area → Matta town → Lalkoo village (the last village on a metalled/semi- metalled road, reachable by ordinary car) → trek up to Gabin Jaba meadows.

Gabin Jaba: "Honey marshes" in Pashto — a genuinely popular local destination (not just an obscure trekker spot), at 8,471ft, 65km from Mingora, now with government-installed camping pods and a winter snow festival.

Daral Lake: From Gabin Jaba, 6-8 hours further trek with about 1,000m of additional ascent — alternatively a 3-4 hour climb direct from Bahrain on bare mountain trail. A small mosque near the lake offers shelter if you'd rather not camp.

Chukail Banda: A newer, recently-publicized meadow in the same Lower Swat area near Gabin Jabba, gaining attention after being shared by KP government officials — still light on formal trekking documentation, so treat it as an add-on to a Gabin Jabba trip rather than a separately-planned destination for now.

Kandol Lake & Spin Khwar Lake

Route: Kalam → Utror (jeep, ~1 hour) → cross a bridge → trek up the valley, 3-4 hours to Kandol Lake, with Spin Khwar (a smaller, less-visited lake) another 2-3 hours beyond/near Kandol — often done together as one long day or overnight.

What it's like: Large green-shaded lake surrounded by snow-covered mountains, often compared to a smaller Saiful Muluk but far less crowded. Moderate-to-difficult day hike, doable without a

guide by confident trekkers but a guide is recommended for the Kandol-to-Spin-Khwar connector specifically.

Izmis Lake & Chambergai (deferred from

Region 1's original misplacement)

Izmis Lake: Southwest of Utror valley, above the treeline — "Izmis" means "caves" in Kohistani, named for natural caves around the lake. Jeep from Utror to Loypanrghalay, then a 3-6 hour trek (one source gives a 13km trail from an 11,230ft start point).

Chambergai Lake: confirmed to sit in the same general Utror valley cluster, frequently mentioned alongside Izmis ("Ismis Banda and Chambergai") — but I couldn't find independent distance/route documentation beyond that pairing. Treat it as a nearby extension of the Izmis trip and confirm the exact split-off point with a guide in Utror.

Mushroom Lake & Andrab Lake (Kalam's high-

alpine side)

Mushroom Lake: In upper Shahi Bagh valley (Gabral), 13,500ft, named for its mushroom-shaped structure — about 31km from Utror or a genuinely long 10-hour hike from Shahi Bagh. One of the harder single-lake objectives on this list distance- wise.

Andrab Lake ("Kooh Lake"): 10,800-11,000ft in Anakar Valley near Kalam, known for visibly shifting from blue to jade-green as the light changes through the day. Route: Kalam Bazaar → jeep 30-45 min to Blue Water Point, Ankar village → 7-8 hour return trek. Arrive by 9-10am for the best color contrast if photography is the goal.

Golen–Bashkargol–Kumrat Traverse

Bashkargol Lake detail: confirmed at 3,652m, a large lake in Chitral district described as looking like a shore or sea in the evening and a still mirror in the morning, about 24km from Sor Laspur settlement on a rugged, steep trail — this is the lake at the heart of this traverse, and can also be reached directly from Sor Laspur without the full Kumrat-side crossing if you just want the lake itself.

What it is: A multi-day traverse starting in the Golen Gol valley of Chitral, crossing Thalo/Thallo Pass (4,180m), passing Bashkargol Lake, and ending in Kumrat Valley — a genuine Chitral-to-Dir crossing, one of the more remote and less- documented multi-day routes on your entire list. Route/days: Thal → Jandrai (gateway village) → Kala Chashma → Shahzore Banda → Zaghi Chatt Lake (camp) → cross Thallo Pass → Bashkargol

Lake → Sor Laspur, Chitral, roughly 6-7 days total, can be pushed to 4-5 by strong trekkers.

Difficulty: Genuinely demanding — 6-12 hour trekking days, a high snow-covered pass crossing at dawn, and full camping/guide/porter support required. This bridges directly into Region 7's Chitral territory, similar to how Region 5's Gujjar Sar Pass bridged Astore and Kashmir.

Zamalo Lakes

What it is: A cluster of at least three (possibly more) glacial lakes below Falaksar Peak, reached from Paloga village — genuinely connects to your visited list, since Paloga/Palogha is one of the spots you've already been to.

Route: Paloga village (~2,500m, just short of Mahodand) → steep, all-ascent trek to Jaba/Jabba summer settlement at the base of Falaksar Peak (3,700m) — a demanding 1,200m single-day climb, with a possible camping spot partway up at the edge of the forest if you'd rather split it over two days.

The lakes: From Jaba, 3-4 more hours to the first three lakes. Zamalo Lake 3 is the biggest and most striking, at 4,300m — a further 600m climb from Jaba. A few more lakes exist above the third one for those with time and stamina to push further.

Difficulty: Genuinely tough for a weekend trek — one trekking account describes doing the whole out-and-back (Paloga → Jaba → lakes → back to Paloga) in essentially two hard days, which they don't recommend unless time-constrained like they were. A 3-day pace with the forest-edge camping option is more sensible.

Practical plus: since it's an out-and-back on the same trail, you can leave a vehicle parked right at Paloga and return straight to it — no need to arrange a pickup elsewhere.

Ansoo Lake. Accessible from the Naran/Saiful Muluk side or from Batakundi via the Dadar Chitta glacier. Trekking to base camp is graded moderate; the actual summit is genuinely dangerous and has had only about 12 successful ascents ever — this is a real mountaineering objective, not a casual trek, above base camp.

Tiger Peak: near Naran, a viewpoint over the valley and Malika Parbat rather than a standalone trekking destination — I found confirmation of its location but no dedicated trek writeups, suggesting it's more of a local sightseeing spot than a formal route.

Musa ka Musalla (deferred from Region 3): 4,060- 4,080m, at the junction of Siran Valley and Kaghan Valley, in Mansehra District — technically its own trek rather than a Kaghan-proper destination. Standard route: Shinkiari → Manda Gucha → Jachha → Dhor → Khori/Gali → summit, typically 3-4 days, though a faster single-day push exists from Balakot with about 1,800m elevation gain in one push if you're already acclimatized. There's a shrine at the summit associated with a shepherd named Musa. Water is only available in the first quarter of the trek — carry enough.

Food: Trout is genuinely the standout here — farmed and river-caught, grilled or fried, sold at hotels and roadside stalls all along the valley, with river trout costing more than farmed and requiring a fishing license if you catch your own. Beyond that it's standard KPK fare done well: chicken/mutton karahi, biryani, and pakora stalls everywhere — nothing as distinctly regional as Hunza's apricot dishes or Baltistan's Balti cuisine, but the trout alone is worth planning a meal around.

Neelum Valley (Azad Kashmir) — already visited, this fills in the specific spots

Getting to Muzaffarabad: Islamabad → Murree/Kohala → Muzaffarabad, about 3-4 hours, then the Neelum Valley road runs upstream: Athmuqam → Sharda → Kel → Keran → Taobat. CNIC is mandatory throughout since the valley runs close to the Line of Control — carry it regardless of how you're traveling.

Bike mechanic in Keran: Jani Bhai — 0355 6318104 — based in Keran, on the road toward Kel; you'll find him just past the hotels on that stretch. Worth saving for the Neelum leg specifically, since Ratti Gali/Arang Kel/Kel are all reached via this same road.

Ratti Gali Lake: About 106-120km from Muzaffarabad via Dowarian, 3,683-3,698m. Jeep to base camp (PKR 5,000-7,000 round trip) then a 40- minute to 2-hour hike to the lake itself. Moderate, beginner-friendly.

Arang Kel: Above Kel village, 2,554m/8,379m elevation, about a 1.5-2.5 hour hike from Kel, or a chairlift for those who'd rather skip the climb — worth staying overnight here rather than in Kel itself, since it's considerably more scenic.

Chitta Katta Lake: In Shounter Valley, Tehsil Sharda, at 4,100m/13,500ft — reached from Kel via a ~20km jeep ride to Domel/Domail then a 5km

trek, typically run as a 4-day round trip with camping. Sits near Mount Hari Parbat, sacred to some Hindu visitors historically (associated with Lord Shiva/Kailash). Described as "a junction of Neelum, Naran, and Skardu" geographically and notably close to the Indian-administered Kashmir border.

Bonus find — Saral Lake: not on your original list, but surfaced in the lakes source you shared and worth flagging since it's in the same valley: a genuinely under-visited lake at 4,100m, reached by descending from the 4,100m Saral Pass into an otherwise-hidden valley, in the same Neelum Valley system as everything else above.

Two corrections found while researching this region

Musa ka Musalla — actually in Mansehra District (Siran Valley/Kaghan junction), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — nowhere near Astore or Gilgit-

Baltistan at all. It's a 4,080m peak reached via Shinkiari → Manda Gucha, a separate 3-4 day trek in its own right. Will cover properly in the Kaghan- Naran-Kashmir region.

Sheitan Gawt Lake — actually in Bahrain Valley, Swat (near Kedam village), not Astore. Will cover in the Swat-Kalam-Kumrat region.

Region 3 is now fully covered.

REGION 4: Gilgit–Naltar–Kohistan

Corridor

Getting there

This is the corridor you already pass through on the way to every other region — Kohistan sits between Besham and Chilas on the KKH, and Gilgit sits right where the Hunza road, Skardu road, Naltar turnoff, and Astore turnoff all meet. If you've already done Region 1's Hunza trip, you've driven through most of this corridor already; this section fills in the side-trips you'd have passed without stopping.

Kohistan — Palas Valley (Morro Meadows & Takhto Lake)

Route: Islamabad → Besham (4-5 hours) → Dobair Bazaar (~15km further) → Pattan (~25km further,

on the KKH) → cross the Indus bridge at Pattan → jeep track into Palas Valley. Kolai-Palas is its own district now, split from the rest of Kohistan, divided into accessible Lower Palas and the harder-to- reach Upper Palas.

Morro (Morro/Morroo) Meadows: From Pattan, a jeep track leads to the village of Khalyar/Shiryal/Mudu (sources vary on the exact village name and route details — this is a genuinely under-documented area), then a trek of roughly 7- 8km with about 1,900m of cumulative elevation gain, taking 3-7 hours depending on the exact route and source. Locals are described as helpful with guiding and porters, though this is not a formal tourism setup — expect to arrange things informally on arrival rather than booking anything in advance.

Takhto Lake (also called Takhto Sar Lake): Also in the Palas Valley cluster, described as one of the least-explored alpine lakes in Pakistan — visited by at least one Pakistani motorbike tour operator specifically as an exploratory trip, which tells you how off the beaten path this still is. I couldn't find hard distance/elevation figures for this one specifically; treat it as bundled with the Morro Meadows trip into the same general Palas Valley area, and expect to figure out final logistics locally.

Bike note: the jeep track from Pattan into Palas Valley is exactly that — a jeep track. Kohistan's

back valleys are some of the least developed for tourism in this entire list, so don't expect the infrastructure (or road quality) you'd find in Hunza or even Kaghan.

Leepa Valley

Accessible from Muzaffarabad, reaching about 10,500ft at Reshian before a jeep descent of ~38km into the valley itself at 5,500ft. Known for terraced fields, apple orchards, and traditional wooden houses — a lower-key cultural/scenic valley rather than a trekking destination, and a separate access road from the main Neelum Valley road.

Neel Fairy Lake, Haveli

What it is: In Forward Kahuta, Haveli District, Azad Kashmir — genuinely Pakistan-administered (not to

be confused with anything across the LOC), in the foothills of Bedori Peak (3,727m/12,228ft). Route: Islamabad → Rawalakot (~109km, 3 hours) → Haveli (~110km further, 4 hours) → Bashan/Suli → Neel Fairy Meadows, with the final stretch being a 2-3 hour trek/hike from where the road ends at around 3,100m elevation for the lake itself.

Notes: Named for the water lily (Neelofer) that grows around it. A genuinely less-visited spot even by AJK standards — worth it if you want somewhere quieter than Neelum Valley's more established circuit.

Important flag: several entries on your list are actually in Indian-administered Kashmir

This isn't a judgment call, it's a practical accessibility fact worth being direct about: the following places from your original list sit across the Line of Control, in Indian-administered Jammu & Kashmir, reached from Srinagar rather than from Pakistan. They are not accessible on a Pakistan-based trip:

Gurez Valley (and Tulail Valley) — Bandipora District, J&K, India, about 123km from Srinagar, reached via Razdan Pass.

Mount Harmukh — 5,142m, Ganderbal District, J&K, India, between Gangabal Lake and the Sindh valley — visible from Gurez but not climbed or approached from anywhere in Pakistan.

Satsar Mala Lakes — Ganderbal District, J&K, India, part of the Kashmir Great Lakes Trek, reached from Sonamarg or Naranag.

Durinar Lakes, Sarbal Village, Sonamarg — Sonamarg itself is in Ganderbal District, J&K, India, so this entire entry sits on the Indian side.

Kausarnag Lake Trek — Kulgam District, J&K, India, in the Pir Panjal range.

I'm flagging these plainly rather than inventing Pakistan-side routes for them, since presenting fake logistics would actively mislead your planning. If any of these matter enough to revisit, that would mean a separate trip through India with an Indian visa and J&K- specific permits — a genuinely different undertaking from the rest of this list.

REGION 3: Astore–Nanga Parbat– Fairy Meadows–Rama

This region turned out smaller than the first two — most of what's on your list here clusters around one mountain (Nanga Parbat) approached from two different sides.

Getting there from Islamabad/Rawalpindi

To Astore town: No single direct route — fly to Gilgit then 4-5 hours by road via Jaglot (120km), or fly to Skardu and cross the Deosai Plain (152km, 4-5 hours, only open roughly June-October), or drive the full KKH to Thalichi near Chilas then the secondary Astore road — about 630km / 15-17 hours total by road.

By bike: the KKH-to-Thalichi-to-Astore route is the one that makes sense on the YBR — same fuel- stop logic as the rest of the KKH corridor

(Mansehra, Besham, Chilas, then the Astore turnoff). The Astore road itself is metalled but narrow, so budget more time than the km count suggests.

By local bus/van: Shared jeeps run Gilgit's Jaglot bus stand to Astore for about PKR 100-1,500 depending on shared vs. special hire, 3-4 hours.

Correction — Minimarg bike rules: My earlier note that motorbikes aren't permitted was wrong. The actual rule: minimum 150cc bikes are allowed into Minimarg — it's bikes under 150cc and regular cars that get turned away; you need either a 4x4 jeep or a 150cc+ bike. This matters directly for you — your Yamaha YBR 125 is a 125cc, under that threshold, so it wouldn't qualify for entry on this specific stretch even though it's fine for the rest of the route to Astore, Rama Meadows, and the broader Deosai/Astore road network. The zone is still militarized and NOC-gated regardless of vehicle: get the NOC from the Assistant Commissioner's office at the start of Rama Road near the Astore lorry depot — bring your bike/car number and CNIC, they'll type and stamp three copies on the spot, then hand copies over at the Army Mess checkpoint on Deosai Road. If you ride the YBR out there, plan to leave it in Astore and go the last stretch by jeep or a rented/borrowed 150cc+ bike.

Rainbow Lake, resolved: this is actually inside Minimarg itself, not a separate Astore-area stop —

an artificial lake built by the Army near Domail/Domel, about 12km past the Minimarg checkpost, known for turquoise water and photogenic surroundings, with nearby Crystal Lake as a bonus stop. So the same 150cc+ rule above applies to reaching it.

Original restriction note (Astore to Minimarg by jeep): Minimarg sits in a heavily militarized zone near the Line of Control, and access requires original CNIC and prior permission, even though it only reopened to general tourists in 2022 after being restricted for 23 years. Astore to Minimarg is about 39km, 3-4 hours by jeep, via Chillam checkpost and Burzil Pass — carry ID for the checkpoints regardless.

Rush Lake Trek

Start point: Hopar/Nagar Valley (via Hoper, roughly 1 hour from Karimabad) — bike-accessible to Hopar.

What it is: Rush Lake sits over 4,700m — Pakistan's highest lake, reached by crossing the Bualtar and Barpu glaciers.

Days: Most itineraries run 7–10 days, though the trekking itself is 5 days of ascent with 2 rest/acclimatization days built in, topping out at a high camp of 4,695m.

Difficulty: Moderate to challenging, mainly due to elevation and terrain rather than technical skill — no specialist climbing skills or gear needed, though the glacier crossings on moraine and exposed ice require care.

Season: June–September.

Notes: A natural add-on if you've already done Rakaposhi — similar region, bigger commitment, genuinely one of the highest lakes you can reasonably walk to in the world.

Patundas Meadows Trek

Start point: Borith Lake (near Passu/Hussaini) — bike-accessible to Borith Lake, then on foot. Route: Borith Lake → Passugar → cross Passu (White) Glacier → Luzhdur/Lazhdar camp → Patundas Meadows.

Distance/elevation: About 29 km total round trip with roughly 2,177m of cumulative elevation gain. Patundas plateau itself sits around 4,170m.

Days: Typically done as a 3-day trek (lower camp → Patundas → back). Difficulty: A mandatory glacier crossing that needs a local guide's route knowledge — not technical, but not something to freelance. The climb from lower camp to Patundas gains around 700m in just a couple of kilometers of steep switchbacks above 3,500m.

Payoff: Views of 16+ peaks over 7,000m including Batura, Passu, Shishper and Rakaposhi, with the Batura and Passu glaciers on either side — regularly rated as one of the best viewpoints in the Karakoram for the effort required.

Guide/access note: Patundas is the property of Ghulkin villagers who hold exclusive portering rights — arrange a guide a day in advance through Ghulkin, or via the Al-Rahim Hotel on the KKH near Gulmit.

Season: May–September.

Kalash Valleys (Bumburet, Rumbur, Birir)

Route from Chitral: Chitral → Ayun (turn-off village) → jeep track into whichever valley, about 35-45km total, 2-3 hours. Bumburet's road is the most reliable/developed; Rumbur and Birir's tracks are narrower, steeper, and more weather-exposed.

Distances from Chitral specifically: Bumburet ~40km, Birir ~34km, Rumbur ~32km, all on jeepable roads.

What's there: The Kalash people — a pre-Islamic, polytheistic culture of roughly 3,000-4,000 people across the three valleys, with distinctive dress, music, and dance, popularly (though not provably) linked in local legend to soldiers from Alexander the Great's army.

Festivals: Chilam Joshi in spring (May), Uchal at harvest time in autumn, and Choimus in winter — these are worth timing a trip around if the cultural side interests you as much as the trekking.

Accommodation: Chitral town has 40+ hotels; Bumburet has 30+, mostly smaller; Rumbur about 6, Birir about 5 — Bumburet is clearly the most set up for visitors of the three.

Etiquette note: this is a living religious minority culture, not a museum exhibit — the usual courtesies (asking before photographing people, dressing modestly, not treating festivals as pure spectacle) apply more than at most other stops on this list.

Golain Valley

About 24km northeast of Chitral town, a large valley bounded by high cliffs, transitioning from forested lower slopes to barren, craggy peaks

higher up. Main settlements: Golain Payeen, Chashma, Bubaka, Izghor, Birmogh, and Istoor.

Activities: Trekking, rock climbing, fishing, and wildlife spotting — genuinely under-developed for tourism, with only one or two local guesthouses currently offering board and lodging. Good camping potential per the same source, but nothing formal yet — this is closer to independent- travel territory than a packaged trek.

→ Shandur/Booni/Mastuj:

Chitral town and Booni (the Upper Chitral hub) are the reliable fuel points on this corridor. Mastuj, Sor Laspur, and the Shandur Pass area itself are small settlements with thin infrastructure — fill up fully at Booni before continuing toward Shandur or into the Yarkhun/Broghil direction.

Neelum Valley:

Muzaffarabad is the main hub. Athmuqam and Kel have basic bazaars and likely fuel, but Taobat (the last village in the valley) and the jeep tracks off the main road (toward Ratti Gali, Arang Kel, Chitta Katta) don't — fill up in Athmuqam or Kel before pushing further up-valley.

The general pattern across every remote jeep-track valley on this list (Chapursan, Shimshal, Naltar, Bilamik/Thorsay, Madaglasht, Hushe): fuel exists in the last KKH/main-road town before the turnoff (Sost for Chapursan, Karimabad/Shishkat area for Shimshal, Nomal for Naltar, the Skardu-road towns for Bilamik, Chitral town for Madaglasht, Khaplu for Hushe) and nowhere beyond it. Treat every side-valley turnoff in this entire document as "last fuel here" unless a specific entry says otherwise.

Connectivity, cash, and seasonal road closures

SIM/network: SCOM is Gilgit-Baltistan's own network and generally has the best coverage in- region — already noted for Neelum specifically but worth knowing as a general rule across GB, not just AJK. Major national networks (Jazz, Zong, Telenor, Ufone) have patchy coverage once you're off the KKH/main roads, and several specific spots in this document (Chapursan, Hushe past Saicho, most

multi-day treks) have no signal at all — that's noted at point of use throughout.

Cash: ATMs exist in Gilgit, Skardu, Hunza (Karimabad/Aliabad), Chitral town, and Mingora — not much beyond that. Carry enough cash for each region's leg before heading into the valleys; jeep hire, guesthouses, and local guides are almost entirely cash transactions.

Seasonal closures, consolidated: Babusar Pass (Kaghan-to-Gilgit link) closes with first winter snow, reopens ~May; Shandur Pass (Chitral-to-Gilgit link) is summer-only; Deosai's road closes to vehicles roughly November-May; Lowari is now tunneled year-round so less of a concern than it used to be, though the old pass itself is still summer-only for those specifically chasing that route. Most individual trek season windows (May/June- September) are already noted per entry — this is just the connecting-road picture.

Swat/Kalam/Malam Jabba/Palogha (already visited — hub notes for what follows)

Kalam is the practical base for almost everything north of it — Utror, Gabral, Matiltan, Mahodand Lake, and the jeep hire point for most of the lakes below. Jeep hire in the area generally runs PKR 3,000-5,000 for a half- day/single destination, up to PKR 10,000-12,000 for longer trips like Mahodand, and budget hotel doubles run roughly PKR 800-1,000 in Mingora, PKR 3,000- 5,000 in Kalam itself.

Kumrat Valley, Jahaz Banda & Katora Lake —

resolving the visited-list question

Good news: these turn out to be the same trek, not two separate lakes — so nothing to untangle. Katora Lake is reached via Jahaz Banda Meadows; Jahaz Banda is the overnight stop and Katora Lake is the destination beyond it, in the upper reaches of Kumrat Valley, Upper Dir District.

Route: Islamabad → Swat Motorway to Chakdara → N-45 through Timergara and Dir → Thal (last town for normal vehicles), ~370-460km, 8-10 hours → jeep from Thal to Taki/Takki Banda, 16km rough track, ~1.5 hours, PKR 5,000 one-way or PKR 10,000-12,000 round trip with overnight → trek 3-5 hours to Jahaz Banda Meadows (camping) → further 3-4 hours to Katora Lake.

Alternative approach from Kalam (Swat side): via Utror → Badgoi Pass → Taki Top, about 3-4 hours, then the same trek onward — genuinely a second valid way in if you're already based in Kalam rather than coming fresh from Islamabad.

Katora Lake: ~3,500m elevation, bowl-shaped (that's what "Katora" means in Pashto), with a smaller "Chota Katora"/Jahaz Banda Lake and a black-stoned spring called Kala Chashma along the way.

Kumrat Waterfall: About 12-13km from Thal, jeep- accessible, requires a short hike to actually see it since it's not visible from the road.

Practical note: no electricity or real food options at Katora Lake itself — carry supplies, and bring a power bank and flashlight. This is genuinely remote-feeling despite being a well-known name.

Qaqlasht Meadows, Booni

Route: Chitral town → Booni, about 80km north, 2- 3 hours by road, then the meadows themselves are close by/around Booni rather than a separate trek beyond it.

What it is: "Qaqlasht" means "dry plain" in Khowar — a broad alpine plateau at roughly 2,300-2,500m with panoramic Hindu Kush views, historically an important communal gathering site for the local Kho people, not just a scenic viewpoint.

Accommodation: Facilities on the meadow itself are basic — camping is the main option. Booni (22km away) has guesthouses/hotels if you'd rather not camp.

Season: May-October, spring for wildflowers specifically.

Shah Jinali Pass & Thui Pass (moved from

Region 6 correction)

What it is: A combined trek in the Hindu Raj range crossing from Upper Chitral into Gilgit-Baltistan — Shah Jinali Pass (called "the King's Polo Ground" locally, 4,259m) connects Rich Gol/Turikho valley with Yarkhun, and Thui Pass (4,499m-4,500m) continues on from Yarkhun into the Yasin Valley, Ghizer District. Route: Chitral → Turikho/Rich Gol valley (jeep) → trek through Shah Jinali Pass → down into Yarkhun valley → cross the Hoghost Bar/Aghost Bar Glacier → Thui Pass → descend into Yasin Valley → jeep to Gilgit. Genuinely one continuous multi-day traverse rather than two separate day trips. Difficulty: Moderately challenging — the two glacier/pass crossings are the demanding sections, otherwise gentle alpine meadow walking; Thui Pass "is just passable" and needs stamina and good health rather than technical climbing skill.

Significance: this is one of the historic trade/connector routes between Chitral and Gilgit- Baltistan — a genuinely different way to link the two halves of Northern Pakistan than the standard Islamabad-KKH-Gilgit loop most people use.

Season: summer only, and the operators combining it with a Kalash valley visit and Chitral

sightseeing suggests it's often packaged as a 2-3 week trip rather than a standalone weekend.

Gear rental & general mechanics

Gear rental in Islamabad: Ascender Outdoors — trekking gear sales and rental (tents, sleeping bags, stoves, crampons, ice axes), F-11/1, Ali Market, Islamabad, +92 333 9980903, info@ascender.pk. Worth stocking up here before heading north rather than counting on finding gear in-valley.

Gear rental in-trek: several specific treks in this document already note local rental (e.g. camping gear at Rakaposhi Base Camp for ~PKR 3,000/night) — those are noted at point of use rather than repeated here.

Mechanics/fuel beyond bike rental shops: every KKH town (Mansehra, Besham, Chilas, Gilgit, Karimabad) and every Swat/Kaghan hub (Mingora, Balakot, Naran, Kalam) has basic mechanics and fuel — mechanics are available in main towns only, so carry basic tools and a spare tube past those points. Past the last town before a jeep track, you're relying on the jeep driver's own mechanical knowledge, which is generally solid since their vehicles take a beating daily.

Jeep hire: this is genuinely how "local guide" works for most of the remote spots in this document — you hire a jeep with driver in the last accessible

town (Thal, Utror, Sassi, Bilamik, Madaglasht, etc.), and the driver either guides you directly or connects you with a local porter/guide on arrival. There's no separate "book a guide in advance" infrastructure for most of these places outside the big-name treks (K2, Rakaposhi, Fairy Meadows) that the tour operators above run as formal packages.

Cultural festivals worth timing a trip around

Nowruz (Nauroze) — March 21-23, celebrated in Gilgit, Hunza, Skardu, and Chitral: polo, football, volleyball, hockey, folk dances and music.

Chilam Joshi — May, Kalash spring festival in Bumburet/Rumbur/Birir, four days of music and dancing — already noted in Region 7.

Ginani — late June/early July, Hunza and Nagar's wheat-harvest festival: orchards, traditional dress, Shina/Burushaski songs, and harissa (a meat-and- wheat dish).

Shandur Polo Festival — 3,700m, the world's highest polo ground, Gilgit vs. Chitral in a free- flowing traditional format dating to 1936, held July 7-9 — accommodation is tent-camping only, book/plan well ahead. Genuinely one of the most spectacular single events on this whole list if the timing works.

Uchal — August, Kalash harvest festival.

Silk Route Festival — Hunza and Ghizer, celebrating the region's Silk Road heritage with traditional music, crafts, and food.

Choimus — December (winter solstice), Kalash's largest festival — cold-weather trip, but a genuinely different experience of the valleys than the summer trekking season this whole document is otherwise built around.

Snow Lake & Hispar La Trek

What it is: A 16km-wide glacial basin at 4,800m where the Biafo and Hispar glaciers meet, connecting Hunza (west) to Baltistan (east) via the Hispar La pass — this is genuinely a cross-region expedition, not a Hunza-only trek.

Two directions: Most groups start from Askole (Skardu side) and finish in Hispar village (Hunza/Nagar side), or occasionally the reverse.

Distance/duration: About 190 km total, 12 days classic itinerary, though full trips including travel run around 3 weeks door to door, with 12 days of high-altitude trekking.

Elevation: Hispar Pass tops out at 5,150m. Difficulty: Strenuous, remote, requires a certified guide and full camping/porter support — no shortcuts here, and no bike or bus gets anywhere near it.

Season: June–September only.

Note for later: we'll cover the Skardu-side approach (Askole, Baltoro) properly when we get to Region 2.

Chapursan Valley & Baldiyat Meadows

Route: KKH to Sost (last town before Khunjerab) → turn off onto the Chapursan valley road → Zood Khun (last village).

Distance/time: About a 4-hour jeep ride from Sost to Zood Khun; roughly 6 hours total from Karimabad, 8 from Gilgit. The Sost–Chapursan road is narrow and rough — not one to underestimate on a loaded bike; go slow and consider it jeep territory past the first villages.

Local transport: One public jeep a day runs the valley, leaving Zood Khun around 5:30–6am — good to know if you're not self-driving.

What's there: Baba Ghundi Shrine (2 hrs beyond Zood Khun), Yishkok Meadow (base for treks toward Yashkuk Yaz Glacier and Sakar Sar base camp, the valley's highest peak at 6,272m), and several scattered Wakhi villages.

Accommodation: Guesthouses and homestays in Zood Khun and nearby villages — basic but authentic Wakhi hospitality.

Best time: June–August, when meadows are in bloom and trails are most accessible. Expect no reliable signal or WiFi once you're past Sost — worth knowing if you're planning to vlog live.

Culture note: If your timing lines up (June– September), Kyrgyz traders sometimes cross from Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor via the Irshad Pass to trade at Chapursan — and there's an annual two-

day Baba Ghundi Festival with traditional games like buzkashi.

Buskochi (Baskochi) Top

Start point: Shishkat village (near Attabad Lake) — bike-accessible.

Route: A 3–4 hour round trip through light forest and traditional Gojal farmland, up to panoramic views of Attabad Lake and the surrounding villages. Difficulty: Easy — a "hidden gem for those who love nature without the burn," good for a late start, sunset trek, or mellow day with local guides.

Good fit for: a half-day add-on if you're already based near Attabad/Hunza and want a viewpoint hike without committing to a full trek day.

Turgil Meadows (Naltar)

What it is: A meadow high in upper Naltar with views of Rakaposhi and Diran in the distance, about a 2-hour trek from upper Naltar.

Geography note: Naltar Valley is technically reached via Nomal (off the KKH before Hunza proper) and administratively sits closer to Gilgit district than Hunza — I'm covering it here since you already know Naltar from your Sheesha Lake visit, but I'll give it fuller treatment (Naltar Lakes/Bashkiri/Satrangi, the ski resort, Naltar- Pakora trek) alongside Kohistan/Gilgit-corridor spots in a later region.

Kho Nagar Valley (Miacher Kho Meadows) —

added after correcting an earlier misplacement

What it is: "Kho Nagar Valley" from your original list is Miacher Kho Meadows (also just called Kho Meadows), a meadow above Miacher village in Nagar Valley — genuinely in Region 1's territory, not Kohistan as I'd first guessed while researching Region 4. Route: Gilgit → Nagar → Minapin → Miacher village → Kho Meadows, about 3-4 hours total from Gilgit City. A short ~30 minute walk from the parking area up to the meadow itself.

Bike note: Explicitly bike-friendly — the source guide's only caution is to tie down luggage tightly given the road condition, unlike most of the harder- to-reach spots in this region. Good road from the KKH turnoff.

What's there: Views toward Diran Peak, Rakaposhi, Hunza's Duikar viewpoint, Hapakun Meadows, and Rakaposhi Base Camp — essentially a lower-effort viewpoint over the same peaks Rakaposhi Base Camp trekkers work much harder to see. Good fit for: an easy day trip if you're already in Minapin for Rakaposhi Base Camp and want a lighter add-on, or a standalone half-day out of Gilgit/Nagar.

Gilgit city

Mostly a waypoint and transport hub rather than a destination in itself — this is where the Hunza road, Skardu road, Naltar turnoff, and Astore turnoff all converge. Gilgit sits about 60km from Astore and roughly 2 hours from Naltar. You've effectively already covered getting here in Region 1's Hunza route section, since Gilgit sits on the same KKH corridor just before the Hunza turnoff. Food-wise, same note as Astore — this is the same broader GB food culture covered in Regions 1 and 2, not a distinct cuisine of its own.

Naltar Valley (fuller treatment — you've already

seen Sheesha Lake here)

Route: Gilgit → Nomal village (turn off the KKH) → Naltar Bala (Upper Naltar), about 34-40km, 1.5-2 hours. The road to Naltar Bala itself is manageable; the lakes beyond require a separate 4x4 jeep leg — old Willys jeeps with reinforced suspension are the standard local vehicle for this stretch, and taking your own vehicle (bike included) isn't advisable for the final rocky, boulder-strewn section.

The lakes: Collectively called the Naltar Lakes or Bashkiri Lakes — Satrangi Lake (Bashkiri I, the famous "seven-colored" one, named for the mix of hues from moss and underwater vegetation), Blue Lake (Bashkiri II, 1km from Satrangi), and Feroza Lake (Bashkiri III), roughly 12-17km from Naltar Bala depending on source.

Jeep costs: Round-trip jeep hire to the lakes runs roughly PKR 15,000-16,000 from Nomal, or about PKR 20,000 one-way if starting the whole trip from Gilgit.

Ski resort: Naltar has Pakistan's oldest ski resort (the other being Malam Jabba in Swat), run largely by the Pakistan Air Force, which introduced skiing here — worth knowing if you're ever up this way in winter instead of summer, since most of this whole document assumes a summer trekking season.

Turgil Meadows recap: as covered back in Region 1 — about a 2-hour trek from upper Naltar, views of Rakaposhi and Diran.

Season: May-October for the lakes/valley in general; winter for skiing.

Diran Peak

What it is: A 7,226m pyramid-shaped peak east of Rakaposhi, first climbed in 1968 by Austrian climbers. Considered the second-easiest 7,000m peak in the Karakoram after Spantik — but has a reputation for avalanches and a notably high death toll for that reason.

Access: Same trailhead as Rakaposhi — Minapin village → Hapakun → Tagaphari → Diran Base Camp at around 3,700m, then Camp I around 5,400m for the actual climb.

Base camp trek only: A round trip from Rakaposhi Base Camp to Diran Base Camp and back takes about 5 hours, crossing the Katchelly Glacier with some genuinely deep crevasses to navigate — this

part is achievable as an add-on to a Rakaposhi trip without full mountaineering gear, though it does require care and ideally a guide.

Full summit: technical climb requiring fixed ropes, ice climbing skills, and multiple high camps — not a casual undertaking.

Season: June–August, and even then avalanche risk is a real factor.

Avgarch & Boibar Valley (Gojal, near Moorkhun)

Start point: Jamalabad, near Moorkhun village on the KKH (about 180km up-river from Gilgit) — inaccessible by any vehicle, foot-only.

Route: A 3–4 hour trek from Jamalabad through Boibar to Avgarch pastures, following the Hunza River's course past rose bushes and side streams.

What's there: Avgarch sits at 3,200m and was the first Wakhi settlement in the area, complete with a mosque with distinctive wood carvings and two old forts. Boibar has spectacular old-growth juniper trees and was historically the route to Shimshal. The ancient Baltar Yarz juniper tree, believed to be several thousand years old, is a highlight along the way. Difficulty: Easy — this one can be done in a single day, unlike most other entries in this region. A good option if you want a genuine Gojal experience without committing to multi-day camping.

Wildlife: Markhor, wolves, and various native birds are seen in the area, which is also managed for regulated trophy hunting in winter.

REGION 4: Gilgit–Naltar–Kohistan

Corridor

Getting there

This is the corridor you already pass through on the way to every other region — Kohistan sits between Besham and Chilas on the KKH, and Gilgit sits right where the Hunza road, Skardu road, Naltar turnoff, and Astore turnoff all meet. If you've already done Region 1's Hunza trip, you've driven through most of this corridor already; this section fills in the side-trips you'd have passed without stopping.

Kohistan — Palas Valley (Morro Meadows & Takhto Lake)

Route: Islamabad → Besham (4-5 hours) → Dobair Bazaar (~15km further) → Pattan (~25km further,

on the KKH) → cross the Indus bridge at Pattan → jeep track into Palas Valley. Kolai-Palas is its own district now, split from the rest of Kohistan, divided into accessible Lower Palas and the harder-to- reach Upper Palas.

Morro (Morro/Morroo) Meadows: From Pattan, a jeep track leads to the village of Khalyar/Shiryal/Mudu (sources vary on the exact village name and route details — this is a genuinely under-documented area), then a trek of roughly 7- 8km with about 1,900m of cumulative elevation gain, taking 3-7 hours depending on the exact route and source. Locals are described as helpful with guiding and porters, though this is not a formal tourism setup — expect to arrange things informally on arrival rather than booking anything in advance.

Takhto Lake (also called Takhto Sar Lake): Also in the Palas Valley cluster, described as one of the least-explored alpine lakes in Pakistan — visited by at least one Pakistani motorbike tour operator specifically as an exploratory trip, which tells you how off the beaten path this still is. I couldn't find hard distance/elevation figures for this one specifically; treat it as bundled with the Morro Meadows trip into the same general Palas Valley area, and expect to figure out final logistics locally.

Bike note: the jeep track from Pattan into Palas Valley is exactly that — a jeep track. Kohistan's

back valleys are some of the least developed for tourism in this entire list, so don't expect the infrastructure (or road quality) you'd find in Hunza or even Kaghan.
